title: "NGS library preparation"

---

How to turn DNA or RNA into a molecule a sequencer can read — and how to design a new way of
doing it when no existing protocol fits.

Self-published course material by Johan Henriksson. It is written for late MSc and PhD
students, and it is self-paced: take the parts you need, in the order you need them. There is
no programming in this course. Exercises are design problems, quizzes and enzyme-selection
tasks, with collapsible **Hint** and **Solution** callouts.

The companion to this course is [NGS 101](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/), a
base-by-base reference for about 840 published library chemistries. Protocols named here link
to their page there.

::: {.callout-note}
This site is being written: the first module is up, the rest is outlined below. The plan for
all of it is in `CURRICULUM.md` in the repository.
:::

## Foundations — what the sequencer needs

Nucleic acids as a building material; how each sequencing platform reads DNA; the anatomy of
a finished library molecule.

**Nucleic acids as a building material** — strand polarity and end states, what a ligase
actually requires, hybridisation and Tm, degenerate bases, oligo modifications, how RNA
differs.

- [Slides](foundations/lectures/nucleic-acids.html)
- [Readings](foundations/lectures/nucleic-acids-readings.html)
- [Exercises](foundations/exercises/nucleic-acids.html)

**How sequencers read DNA** — clustering and sequencing by synthesis, the four reads and
their order, i5 orientation, insert size versus read length, index hopping and base
diversity; then MGI, AVITI, Ultima, PacBio and Nanopore, and what each asks of a library.

- Slides: [How Illumina reads DNA](foundations/lectures/sequencers-illumina.html) ·
  [The other sequencing platforms](foundations/lectures/sequencers-other.html)
- [Readings](foundations/lectures/sequencers-readings.html)
- [Exercises](foundations/exercises/sequencers.html)

*Coming: anatomy of a library molecule*

## Building blocks

The core of the course. One module per step you can put into a protocol: the enzyme toolbox,
attaching a handle, end chemistry, fragmentation, amplification, selection, barcodes and UMIs,
converting chemistry into sequence, and compartments. Each covers what the step does to the
molecule, how it fails, and the tricks practitioners use.

## Use cases

Whole protocols read as combinations of blocks: genomic DNA, RNA, targeted sequencing,
chromatin, the 3D genome, modifications, single cells, spatial, pooled screens, long reads.

## The trick catalogue

Cross-cutting reference, indexed by the problem rather than by the step: making the right
thing ligate, killing what you do not want, getting a handle onto an impossible end, counting
honestly, working with degraded material.

## Quality control and designing your own

Cleanups, quantification and reading a trace; design patterns and failure modes; a capstone
where you design a library prep from scratch.
